title: US and Denmark Reach Deal on Greenland After Trump's Threats
summary:
For months, President Donald Trump said he wanted to take control of Greenland, a huge icy island in the Arctic. He even threatened to seize it by force. That made people in Greenland and Denmark very upset. Earlier this year, Greenlanders protested in their capital, Nuuk.

But on Saturday, the US and Denmark announced a deal. Trump said Denmark would give the US "permanent control over security, and all other needs" in Greenland. He also said no US adversary could have a military presence there without US approval. The deal, he said, comes at "no cost to the United States."

Denmark's Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen welcomed the deal. They said it would "strengthen security" in the Arctic and the North Atlantic. It also recognizes "the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination." That means Greenland stays part of Denmark, and its people get to decide their own future.

Nato, a military alliance of 32 countries, welcomed the deal. A spokesperson said it would "help advance security, stability and cooperation in this vital region."

French President Emmanuel Macron said the deal helped "reaffirm Danish sovereignty" over the island. "Danish sovereignty is respected, international law is respected," he said.

The deal is expected to be signed next week at the UN General Assembly. But no text has been released yet, so nobody knows all the details. It still needs to go through parliamentary procedures to take effect.
why_it_matters: Countries often argue about land and who controls it, and this story shows how talking and signing an agreement can settle a big fight instead of using force — a lesson that works for disagreements at home or at school too.

keywords.explanation: A huge icy island in the Arctic, mostly covered in ice, that is part of the Kingdom of Denmark.
The right of a country or people to rule themselves without another country telling them what to do.
The right of a group of people to decide their own future and how they will be governed.
A military alliance — a team of 32 countries that promise to defend each other.
The steps a deal or law must go through in a country's lawmaking group before it can take effect.

background_read: Greenland is the world's largest island, sitting mostly inside the Arctic Circle between North America and Europe; it is not its own country but a self-governing territory of Denmark.
The United States has had a military base in Greenland for many decades, and the island's position makes it important for watching the Arctic and the North Atlantic.

Nato (the North Atlantic Treaty Organization) was created so that countries in Europe and North America would defend each other if one of them were attacked — the United States and Denmark are both members.
Article_Structure: WHO: President Donald Trump, Denmark's Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen, Nato, and French President Emmanuel Macron.

WHAT: After months of threats, the US and Denmark announced a deal giving the US 'permanent control over security, and all other needs' in Greenland, while Greenland stays part of Denmark and keeps its right to self-determination.
WHERE: Greenland, a huge Arctic island, with the deal expected to be signed next week at the UN General Assembly.
WHY: The deal is meant to end months of threats and protests and to strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic, but the details are still secret.

perspectives.description: They welcomed the deal, saying it strengthens security in the Arctic and North Atlantic while still recognizing that Greenland belongs to Denmark and its people decide their own future.
Many were upset when Trump talked about taking the island, and some may worry that giving the US 'permanent control over security' hands too much power over their home to another country.

They see the deal as a way to keep peace in a vital region and to respect international law and Danish sovereignty, though Macron stressed that Danish sovereignty is respected only because the deal keeps Greenland with Denmark.
